q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Number so the multiple bonds as a set get the lowest locants. If both directions tie, which multiple bond wins the lower number?
w: Both numbering directions give the multiple bonds locants {1,4}. When there is a tie, IUPAC gives the double bond the lower number, so the name is pent-1-en-4-yne. In an enyne name the "-en-" always comes before the "-yne" (alphabetical order of the endings), and the final "e" of "-ene" is dropped.
x: This numbering gives the same locant set {1,4} but puts the lower number on the triple bond; on a tie the double bond gets the lower number.
In an enyne name "-ene" is cited first and "-yne" last; "-yn-...-ene" is never used.
Every multiple bond needs its own locant, written next to its own ending; a combined "1,4-enyne" ending is not used.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: First find the lowest locant set for both multiple bonds; only use the "double bond gets the lower number" rule if the sets tie. Then assign E/Z.
w: Numbering from the alkyne end gives locants {1,3}; from the other end {2,4}. The first point of difference decides, so C1 is the alkyne carbon: (E)-pent-3-en-1-yne. The double-bond tiebreaker only applies when the locant sets are equal, which they are not here. At C3=C4 the higher-priority groups (the alkynyl carbon on C3 and the CH3 on C4) are on opposite sides, so the alkene is E.
x: The two higher-priority groups (C≡CH on C3, CH3 on C4) are on opposite sides of the double bond, which is E, not Z.
Locants {2,4} are higher than {1,3}; the double bond gets the lower number only when the two sets tie.
The ending order is always "-en-...-yne"; "-yn-...-ene" is not an IUPAC form.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Settle the numbering using the multiple bonds first (lowest set, then the double bond lower). Substituent locants are considered only after that.
w: The six-carbon chain holds both multiple bonds. From either end the multiple bonds get {1,5}, a tie, so the double bond gets C1. Numbering from the alkene end puts the methyl on C4: 4-methylhex-1-en-5-yne. The ene-before-substituent priority means you cannot renumber just to give the methyl a lower locant (3).
x: This numbers from the alkyne end to give the methyl locant 3, but the double-bond tiebreaker outranks substituent locants.
Locant 3 for the methyl would require numbering from the alkyne end, which would make the alkene C5, not C1; the name mixes two numberings.
Numbering from the alkyne end makes the alkene C5 and the methyl C3, not C4; and the double bond should get the lower number anyway.

q: A terminal alkyne (pKa ≈ 25) must be converted completely to its acetylide ion before an alkylation. Which base is suitable?
h: An acid–base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid. Compare the pKa of the alkyne with the pKa of each base's conjugate acid.
w: Deprotonation is favorable only if the conjugate acid of the base is a weaker acid (higher pKa) than the alkyne. NH3 (38) is far weaker than the alkyne (25), so NaNH2 deprotonates it essentially completely (Keq ≈ 1013). Hydroxide, ethoxide and bicarbonate all have conjugate acids stronger than the alkyne, so the equilibrium lies on the alkyne side.
x: Water (15.7) is a much stronger acid than the alkyne (25), so hydroxide leaves the alkyne almost entirely protonated (Keq ≈ 10−9).
Ethanol (16) is a stronger acid than the alkyne, so ethoxide gives only a trace of acetylide; this is the classic "close enough" trap.
Bicarbonate is a very weak base; carbonic acid (6.4) is about 10<sup>18</sup> times more acidic than the alkyne.

q:
Which list puts these compounds in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first)?
ethane, ethene, ethyne, ammonia
h: For the hydrocarbons, think about the s character of the orbital holding the lone pair in each conjugate base. Then place NH3 using its pKa (≈ 38).
w: Approximate pKa values: ethane ≈ 50 (sp3, 25% s), ethene ≈ 44 (sp2, 33% s), ammonia ≈ 38, ethyne ≈ 25 (sp, 50% s). More s character holds the carbanion lone pair closer to the nucleus, stabilizing the base. So ethane < ethene < ammonia < ethyne. This ordering is why NH2− deprotonates a terminal alkyne but not an alkene.
x: Ethyne (25) is far more acidic than ammonia (38); if ammonia were the stronger acid, NaNH<sub>2</sub> could not make acetylides.
Ammonia (38) is more acidic than ethane (50) and ethene (44); N is more electronegative than C.
Ethene (sp2, pKa ≈ 44) is more acidic than ethane (sp3, ≈ 50), not less.

q: Which statement best describes the equilibrium shown (pKa: ethyne ≈ 25, ethanol ≈ 16)?
c: It lies far to the left; Keq ≈ 10−9
It lies far to the right; Keq ≈ 109
It lies far to the left; Keq ≈ 10−41
It is roughly balanced; Keq ≈ 1, because both acids are weak
h: For HA + B− ⇌ A− + HB, log Keq = pKa(HB) − pKa(HA).
w: The acid on the left is ethyne (25); the acid on the right is ethanol (16). Keq = 10(16 − 25) = 10−9, far to the left. Equilibrium favors the weaker acid (ethyne) and weaker base (ethoxide). That is why ethoxide cannot be used to make acetylide ions for alkylation.
x: This inverts the subtraction; equilibrium favors the weaker acid, and ethyne (25) is weaker than ethanol (16).
The exponent comes from the difference of pKa values (16 − 25 = −9), not their sum.
Both are weak acids, but they differ by 9 pKa units, so Keq is nowhere near 1.

q: What is the major organic product of this sequence?
h: Step 1 makes a carbon nucleophile at the terminal carbon. Where does the new C–C bond form, and how many carbons does each piece bring?
w: NaNH2 removes the terminal ≡C–H of propyne. The acetylide carbon attacks the primary carbon of 1-bromobutane by SN2, joining C3 + C4 = 7 carbons with the triple bond kept where it was: CH3C≡C–CH2CH2CH2CH3, hept-2-yne.
x: Hept-1-yne would need the butyl group on the internal carbon; the new bond forms at the deprotonated terminal carbon, so the triple bond ends up internal (C2).
This has the triple bond at C3, which would require an ethyl acetylide and a propyl halide; propyne + butyl gives the triple bond between C2 and C3.
A branched product would require attack at a secondary carbon; S<sub>N</sub>2 at the primary C–Br gives an unbranched chain.

q: Sodium propynide is treated with 2-bromopropane in liquid NH<sub>3</sub>. What is the main outcome?
c: E2: propene forms and propyne is regenerated
S<sub>N</sub>1: 4-methylpent-2-yne forms through an isopropyl cation
No reaction: acetylides do not react with alkyl halides
h: An acetylide is a strong base as well as a nucleophile. What does a strong base usually do with a secondary alkyl halide?
w: Acetylide ions are strong bases (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 25). With a secondary (or tertiary) halide, backside attack is hindered and E2 wins: the acetylide removes a β-H from 2-bromopropane, giving propene, Br−, and propyne (the acetylide is protonated). Acetylide alkylation is used only with methyl and primary halides.
x: S<sub>N</sub>2 at a secondary carbon is slow, and the strongly basic acetylide prefers E2 there, so little or no 4-methylpent-2-yne forms.
A secondary halide does not ionize in NH<sub>3</sub> with a strong base present; the strong base reacts bimolecularly (E2) instead.
Acetylides do react with alkyl halides: S<sub>N</sub>2 with methyl/primary halides and E2 with secondary/tertiary ones.

q: Which route gives the best yield of the alkyne shown?
h: There are two ways to disconnect the target at a C(sp)–C(sp<sup>3</sup>) bond. Which disconnection puts the halide on a carbon that can do S<sub>N</sub>2?
w: The target is 4,4-dimethylpent-2-yne, (CH3)3C–C≡C–CH3. Disconnecting the CH3–C≡ bond uses the tert-butyl acetylide (from 3,3-dimethylbut-1-yne and NaNH2) plus CH3I, a methyl halide that reacts cleanly by SN2: 3,3-dimethylbut-1-yne; 1. NaNH2 2. CH3I. The other disconnection would need a tert-butyl halide, which gives only E2 with acetylides.
x: A tertiary halide cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2; the acetylide acts as a base and gives isobutylene (E2).
Neopentyl bromide is primary but too hindered for S<sub>N</sub>2, and it would add an extra CH<sub>2</sub> (C8 product, not the C7 target).
Hydroxide cannot deprotonate a terminal alkyne (water, pKa 15.7, is the stronger acid), so almost no acetylide forms.

q: Pent-1-yne is made from 1,2-dibromopentane with 3 equivalents of NaNH<sub>2</sub>, followed by H<sub>2</sub>O. Why are 3 equivalents of base needed rather than 2?
c: Pent-1-yne (pKa ≈ 25) is deprotonated by NaNH2, using a third equivalent; H2O then reprotonates it.
The third equivalent isomerizes the pent-2-yne that forms first into the terminal alkyne, pent-1-yne.
Each E2 step needs two equivalents of base because NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> removes both a proton and a bromide.
The third equivalent converts the vinyl bromide intermediate into an amine, which then eliminates NH<sub>3</sub>.
h: Count the base used by the two eliminations. Then ask what NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> does to the product itself.
w: Two E2 reactions (each uses one NH2−) convert the vicinal dibromide to the alkyne. But a terminal alkyne (pKa 25) is far more acidic than NH3 (38), so the product is immediately deprotonated by a third equivalent. The final H2O workup protonates the acetylide to release pent-1-yne. (For an internal alkyne, 2 equivalents suffice.)
x: From a 1,2-dibromide the triple bond forms between C1 and C2 directly; no isomerization step is needed or intended.
Each E2 uses one base: the base takes the β-H and bromide leaves on its own as Br<sup>−</sup>.
Amide is not acting as a nucleophile on the vinyl bromide here; the second step is another E2.

q: Which dibromide gives pent-1-yne as the main product with 3 equiv NaNH2, then H2O?
h: Double dehydrohalogenation forms the triple bond between the carbons that carry the bromines (vicinal) or between the C–Br carbon and its neighbor (geminal).
w: The two E2 steps create the triple bond between the two carbons that lose the H–Br pairs. For a C1≡C2 triple bond, the bromines must be on C1 and C2 (vicinal) or both on C1 or C2 (geminal). 1,2-Dibromopentane fits. 2,3- and 3,3-dibromopentane place the triple bond at C2–C3 (pent-2-yne), and 1,3-dibromopentane cannot form a triple bond at all because its bromines are not on the same or adjacent carbons.
x: Bromines on C2 and C3 give the triple bond between C2 and C3: pent-2-yne, not pent-1-yne.
A geminal dibromide at C3 can eliminate only toward C2 or C4; both give pent-2-yne.
The bromines are on C1 and C3, so the two eliminations cannot build two π bonds between one pair of carbons; a diene or other products form instead.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: Lindlar's catalyst is a "poisoned" catalyst. How many H<sub>2</sub> add, and from which face?
w: Lindlar's catalyst (Pd on CaCO3, poisoned with lead acetate and quinoline) adds one equivalent of H2 syn from the metal surface and stops at the alkene. Hex-3-yne gives (Z)-hex-3-ene.
x: The E alkene comes from dissolving-metal reduction (Na, NH3), not from syn addition on a catalyst surface.
Full reduction to the alkane happens with an active catalyst such as Pt or Pd/C; the poisoned Lindlar catalyst stops at the alkene.
Hydrogenation adds H atoms to the two alkyne carbons; it does not move the double bond to C2.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: Dissolving-metal reductions add electrons one at a time. Which alkene geometry results, and how is the alkene numbered?
w: Na in liquid NH3 adds two electrons and two protons anti, giving the trans (E) alkene and stopping there. 4-Methylpent-2-yne gives CH3CH=CH–CH(CH3)2; numbering from the end nearer the double bond gives (E)-4-methylpent-2-ene.
x: The Z (cis) alkene is the Lindlar (H2, syn) product; Na/NH3 gives the E alkene.
Na/NH<sub>3</sub> does not reduce isolated alkenes, so the reaction stops at the alkene.
This is the correct alkene numbered from the wrong end; the double bond must get the lower locant (2, not 3).

h: Br2 adds anti to an alkene. For a symmetric alkene, does anti addition to the cis or the trans isomer give the meso product?
w: Bromine adds anti through a bromonium ion. Anti addition to trans-but-2-ene gives the meso (2R,3S) dibromide, while anti addition to cis-but-2-ene gives the racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair. So make the trans alkene first with dissolving metal: 1. Na, NH3(l) 2. Br2.
x: Lindlar gives cis-but-2-ene; anti addition of Br2 to the cis alkene gives the racemic (R,R)/(S,S) dibromide, not meso.
H<sub>2</sub>/Pt reduces the alkyne all the way to butane, which has no π bond for Br<sub>2</sub> to add to.
Two equivalents of HBr add Markovnikov to give the geminal 2,2-dibromobutane, not a vicinal dibromide.

q: What is the major product when pent-1-yne reacts with 2 equivalents of HBr (no peroxides)?
h: Each HBr adds Markovnikov. After the first addition, which carbocation is stabilized by the bromine already present?
w: The first HBr adds Markovnikov to give 2-bromopent-1-ene. In the second addition, H+ adds to C1 so the cation forms at C2, where the bromine lone pair stabilizes it by resonance. Bromide then adds to C2, giving the geminal dihalide 2,2-dibromopentane.
x: A vicinal (1,2) dibromide comes from Br<sub>2</sub> addition, not from two HBr additions.
Putting both Br on C1 is anti-Markovnikov; without peroxides H adds to C1 each time.
This is the product of only one equivalent of HBr; with 2 equivalents the vinyl bromide adds a second HBr.

q: What is the final organic product of this reaction?
h: Mercury-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov, and the first product is not stable. What does it tautomerize to?
w: HgSO4/H2SO4 adds water Markovnikov: OH goes to C2 of hex-1-yne, giving the enol CH2=C(OH)C4H9. The enol tautomerizes to the more stable keto form, hexan-2-one.
x: An aldehyde comes from anti-Markovnikov hydration (disiamylborane or 9-BBN, then H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>/NaOH), not from HgSO<sub>4</sub>.
Alkyne hydration gives a carbonyl compound, not an alcohol; nothing reduces the C=O here.
This enol is the first-formed intermediate, but it tautomerizes to the ketone under the acidic conditions.

q: Which alkyne gives a single ketone on hydration with HgSO4, H2SO4, H2O?
h: For an internal alkyne, the OH can end up on either sp carbon. When do both choices give the same compound?
w: An internal alkyne with two different alkyl groups has no strong Markovnikov preference, so it gives a mixture of two ketones. A symmetric internal alkyne gives the same ketone either way. Hex-3-yne gives only hexan-3-one.
x: Hex-2-yne gives both hexan-2-one and hexan-3-one, because its two sp carbons are both disubstituted.
The isopropyl and ethyl groups differ, so 2-methylhex-3-yne gives a mixture of 2-methylhexan-3-one and 5-methylhexan-3-one.
Oct-3-yne has an ethyl and a butyl group, so it gives octan-3-one and octan-4-one.

q: What is the final organic product of this sequence? (Sia<sub>2</sub>BH = disiamylborane)
h: Hydroboration puts boron on the less substituted carbon. After oxidation, the OH is on a C=C carbon. What happens to that?
w: Disiamylborane adds once, with boron on the terminal carbon (anti-Markovnikov, syn). H2O2/NaOH replaces B with OH, giving the enol CH3CH2CH2CH=CH–OH, which tautomerizes to the aldehyde: pentanal.
x: The methyl ketone is the Markovnikov product of HgSO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> hydration.
No reducing agent is present; the enol tautomerizes to an aldehyde, which is not reduced to the alcohol.
This enol is the intermediate formed by oxidation; it tautomerizes to the aldehyde.
